highlights: 今日技术圈焦点集中在AI发展路径的转向与底层科学的融合。业界正逐渐从单纯的智力比拼转向更看重模型的推理速度与实际应用，同时AI在数学等理论科学领域的突破引发了关于“无数学家数学”的广泛讨论。此外，大型科技公司内部的职场文化与功劳分配问题成为热议话题，折射出行业对组织生态的关注。在工程与历史维度，开发者工具的迭代与对早期计算历史的回顾，也展现了技术圈对基础建设与传承的持续探索。

blocks.text: Open letters about AI development
I wrote this summary of the past few weeks of open letters as a section of my sponsors-only newsletter but I've decided to share it here as well.

Open Weights and American AI Leadership was shepherded by Microsoft, dated July 24th, and signed by 235 AI-adjacent companies including NVIDIA (see Jensen's first ever tweet), Amazon, Y Combinator, The Linux Foundation, and (a later signer) OpenAI.

It's clearly an argument designed to counter any instincts by the current US government to ban or limit open weight models over "safety" concerns - a reasonable consideration given what happened to Claude Fable 5!

Relying solely on closed models is not inherently safe: they can be breached, misused, or fail in ways that outsiders cannot detect. And concentrating advanced AI capabilities behind a small number of closed models compounds that risk. It results in a small number of single points of failure, weakens competition, and leaves critical technology in the hands of a few providers. Open weight models, on the other hand, allow a broad community of researchers and developers to examine their behavior, identify vulnerabilities, develop safeguards, and improve them over time.
The one surprising note in the letter is that it comes out in support of distillation, where models train on output from other models:

In shaping this ecosystem, policymakers should be careful not to conflate legitimate model-development techniques with misappropriation. Distillation, or the practice of using one model’s outputs to help train or improve another, is a widely used technique for model improvement, evaluation, and validation. It reflects a long tradition of learning from, building upon, and improving existing technologies, a tradition that has helped drive innovation since the rise of the open-source software movement.

Notably absent from the signatures: Anthropic, who published their own response Our position on open-weights models three days later. CEO Dario Amodei doubled down on the risk of authoritarian governments building "AI models that are more powerful than those built by the US", and models being "misused to carry out cyberattacks or biological attacks", and called for "a crack down on industrial-scale distillation operations", while also stating that "Anthropic has never advocated for a ban on open-weights models".

Then on July 28th Pacing the Frontier was published, featuring signatures from "1,324 employees of frontier AI companies" - with names like Jakub Pachocki (Chief Scientist, OpenAI), Ilya Sutskever (Safe Superintelligence Inc, previously OpenAI), Dario Amodei (Anthropic), Jack Clark (Anthropic) and more. Their core message:
We request that the U.S. government support an international effort to develop the technical and governance tools needed to deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development.

Their concern is intense competitive pressure combined with accelerated AI progress caused by automated AI research - and given that Anthropic produce 80% of their code with Claude Code, OpenAI had Sol reduce their end-to-end serving costs by 20%, and Kimi K3 designed a chip to serve a nano model built on its own architecture, you can see why people are taking that risk more seriously right now.

translations: 关于 AI 发展的公开信
我把过去几周关于公开信的总结写成了赞助者专属通讯的一个部分，但我决定也在这里分享出来。
《开放权重与美国 AI 领导力》由 Microsoft 牵头，日期为 7 月 24 日，共有 235 家与 AI 相关的公司签署，包括 NVIDIA（参见 Jensen 的第一条推文）、Amazon、Y Combinator、The Linux Foundation，以及（后来的签署者）OpenAI。
这显然是一个旨在反驳当前美国政府出于“安全”考虑而禁止或限制开放权重模型本能的论点——考虑到 Claude Fable 5 发生的事情，这是一个合理的考量！
仅仅依赖闭源模型本身并不安全：它们可能会被攻破、滥用，或者以局外人无法察觉的方式发生故障。将先进的 AI 能力集中在少数闭源模型背后会加剧这种风险。这会导致少数单点故障，削弱竞争，并将关键技术掌握在少数提供商手中。另一方面，开放权重模型允许广泛的研究人员和开发者社区检查其行为，识别漏洞，开发安全防护措施，并随着时间的推移对其进行改进。
这封信中令人惊讶的一点是，它公开支持蒸馏技术，即模型基于其他模型的输出进行训练：
在塑造这一生态系统时，政策制定者应小心，不要将合法的模型开发技术与盗用混为一谈。蒸馏，即使用一个模型的输出来帮助训练或改进另一个模型的做法，是一种广泛用于模型改进、评估和验证的技术。它反映了从现有技术中学习、在其基础上构建并加以改进的悠久传统，这一传统自开源软件运动兴起以来一直推动着创新。
签名中明显缺席的是 Anthropic，他们在三天后发表了自己的回应《我们对开放权重模型的立场》。CEO Dario Amodei 强调了威权政府构建“比美国构建的更强大的 AI 模型”的风险，以及模型被“滥用于实施网络攻击或生物攻击”的风险，并呼吁“打击工业规模的蒸馏操作”，同时声称“Anthropic 从未主张禁止开放权重模型”。
随后在 7 月 28 日，《把握前沿节奏》发表，署名者包括“1,324 名前沿 AI 公司的员工”——其中包括 Jakub Pachocki（OpenAI 首席科学家）、Ilya Sutskever（Safe Superintelligence Inc，前 OpenAI）、Dario Amodei（Anthropic）、Jack Clark（Anthropic）等人。他们的核心信息是：
我们请求美国政府支持一项国际努力，以开发有意识地把握自动化 AI 发展前沿所需的技术和治理工具。
他们担心的是激烈的竞争压力与自动化 AI 研究导致的 AI 进步加速相结合——考虑到 Anthropic 用 Claude Code 生成了他们 80% 的代码，OpenAI 让 Sol 将其端到端服务成本降低了 20%，而 Kimi K3 设计了一款芯片来服务于基于其自身架构构建的 nano 模型，你就能明白为什么人们现在更加严肃地对待这种风险了。

articles.title: I'm (mostly) picking models on speed now, not intelligence
articles.titleZh: I'm (mostly) picking models on speed now, not intelligence
articles.summary: I'm (mostly) picking models on speed now, not intelligence

blocks.text: For the first time I can remember, I'm not choosing my daily driver models on raw intelligence. I'm choosing them on speed.
Have we reached an intelligence tipping point?

This is probably going to age like spoilt milk, but right now, models around the ~Opus 4.6 level seem to be 'smart enough' for most of my daily tasks - code, pulling together research, designing slide decks and doing analytical tasks against a plethora of databases.

While like most I was hyped to play around with Fable, ironically the US Gov shutdown gave everyone time to get used to Opus again. When Fable came back post-hype with additional guardrails, the first thing I noticed was just how slow it is[1]. So slow, actually, that I switched back to Opus pretty quickly.

I've spent a lot of my career making software fast. It's remarkable how much better software feels to interact with when it's fast. In my experience (and many studies), you can take the most beautiful product, but if it's slow, you won't enjoy using it. Equally, you can take a very basic product that's super fast and it will feel brilliantly utilitarian. [2]

It's clear to me that when only a few, big, slow models cleared the aforementioned (and hypothetical) intelligence bar, it wasn't worth the trade off really to use a slower model. Whatever speed you gain you quickly lose in having to redo it because it was broken.
Is 100tok/s the new 100ms?
I've written before about agents feeling like dialup, back when frontier models were crawling along at 30-60tok/s. That has changed faster than I expected.

The key fact I remember is that to humans, ~100ms feels 'instant', the gold standard. I reckon 100tok/s output on a model is about as fast as I can keep up with. After that, it comes in faster than I can (skim) read. This isn't an exact bar, because increasingly most of the model time is spent in reasoning, and not actually showing you output tokens. And also it massively varies on your output, prose gets output with far fewer tokens per character than code, so your mileage may (and will) vary.

But roughly, 100-200tok/s to me seems pretty damn fast. Below 50tok/s output feels increasingly slow. Ironically, going past 200tok/s seems almost unnerving - you can try a model out here at 10,000tok/s+ (!). I'm sure this feeling will edge upwards as we get used to it and push our agents to do more complicated work.

Given the plethora of new models that I think are ~clearing the aforementioned bar - such as GLM5.2 and DeepSeek V4 Flash GA - that are open weights and small(er), we now have a wide range of models and speed. If you look at the speed rankings of various providers for GLM5.2 on OpenRouter you can see the enormous range of serving speed - from less than 30tok/s at the bottom to 129tok/s at the top.

This is another huge plus to the open weights ecosystem. While there are great benefits in cost that are obvious, the fact that providers are also incentivised to compete on speed like this is really interesting.[3]
But there are limitations
If you're familiar with Pareto's Principle and Amdahl's Law you'll know what's coming up.
Assuming "good enough" models continue to get faster and faster, increasingly the speed benefit is lost to tool calls, and us humans overseeing them.

Take an agent using a model processing at 50tok/s. Most of the time is spent waiting for inference to come back. Now run the same turn at 250tok/s and you'll see that increasingly you are bottlenecked on tool calls on your "local" machine and your decision making.
Rough numbers, but the shape holds. The 5x speedup on the model only buys you a 2x speedup on the turn, because the other 25 seconds didn't move.

And even worse, making your local machine faster on these tool calls is sort of stalling out, because hardware costs have gone parabolic because of AI. Yet again another weird derivative effect of the AI market.

So I suspect (for now at least) there is a limit to how much demand there will be for speed, past a certain point. No doubt there'll be some examples where huge amounts of reasoning are useful (like mathematics research), and speeding that up is helpful. But I'd expect many agents to start getting bottlenecked on your local/internal hardware, database calls and other bits of latency.
The price war is coming

Interestingly OpenAI reduced the cost of their Luna variant by 80% just before the DeepSeek V4 Flash GA release, making it remarkably affordable for a frontier model. While I haven't had as much luck with getting great output out of it vs GLM5.2, I think it points towards an absolute bloodbath of pricing at this end of the market.
You can see this happening on OpenRouter with GLM5.2 - endless discounts being offered to try and attract customers in. We're already down to $0.42/$1.32/MTok on GLM5.2 - 5% of the price of Opus.
While the very cheapest is slow, for not much more you can get 109tok/s from DeepInfra.

As the next generation set of GPUs start being deployed over the next few months - Nvidia's Vera Rubin series and AMD's MI400s, amongst others - the new HBM4 memory in those chips will deliver a 2x+ speedup on output tokens from memory bandwidth alone, plus more on top from additional compute and interlink.

In 2027 it's very possible we'll have very good quality models, at reasonable prices running at 500tok/s+. Staring at "still thinking on xhigh effort" for most of your day may finally become a thing of the past.

What will be interesting to watch for - and I'm not sure where to bet - is if the vast 2-3T+ param models actually do perform dramatically better for everyday tasks. On one hand it feels like we've hit a sweet spot right now, on another having an order of magnitude more intelligence in the model may make that sweet spot look very, very primitive.

Second of course is the endless guardrails firing, which tend to happen at the worst possible time - just when I'm getting deep into a difficult task and I feel I could do with the extra "firepower" that Fable offers, but that's a story for another day. ↩︎

A classic example is something like Craigslist or Hacker News. While they look dated, they are so damn responsive you don't notice. Equally, your "standard" SPA app serving 30MB of React to render a homepage feels like treacle and a chore to use most of the time, despite what was surely an enormous spend on design and product. ↩︎

I'm aware that both OpenAI and Anthropic have offered fast variants of models for a long time, but the API pricing is eye watering. Unless you are tokenmaxxing your benchmarks with a blank cheque, I haven't come across anyone that uses them for day to day operation. Having great models that are super fast at a reasonable price is a very recent addition to the market. ↩︎

translations: 在我记忆中，这是我第一次不根据原始智能来选择日常主力模型，而是根据速度来选择。
我们是否已经达到了智能的临界点？
这句话可能很快就会像变质牛奶一样过时，但就目前而言，智能水平在 Opus 4.6 左右的模型似乎已经“足够聪明”，可以胜任我大部分的日常任务——编写代码、汇总研究、设计幻灯片，以及针对大量数据库进行分析任务。
虽然和大多数人一样，我对试用 Fable 感到兴奋，但讽刺的是，美国政府的停摆给了大家重新适应 Opus 的时间。当 Fable 在热度消退后带着额外的护栏回归时，我注意到的第一件事就是它太慢了[1]。实际上，它慢到我很快就切回了 Opus。
我的职业生涯中有很多时间都在致力于让软件变快。当软件运行迅速时，交互体验的提升是显而易见的。根据我的经验（以及许多研究），即使是最精美的产品，如果运行缓慢，你也不会喜欢使用它。同样，一个非常基础但速度极快的产品，也会让人感觉极其好用。[2]
我很清楚，当只有少数几个庞大且缓慢的模型能够达到前述（假设的）智能标准时，使用较慢的模型其实并不值得。你获得的任何速度优势，都会因为模型出错而不得不重做，从而迅速丧失。
100tok/s 是新的 100ms 吗？
我以前写过，当前沿模型还在以 30-60tok/s 的速度缓慢爬行时，智能体感觉就像拨号上网一样。这种情况改变得比我预期的要快。

我记得的一个关键事实是，对人类来说，大约 100ms 的延迟感觉就是“瞬间”的，这是黄金标准。我认为模型 100tok/s 的输出速度大约是我能跟上的极限。超过这个速度，它的输出就比我（略读）的速度还要快了。这并不是一个精确的标准，因为现在模型的大部分时间都花在了推理上，而不是实际向你展示输出的 token。而且这也很大程度上取决于你的输出内容，散文每个字符输出的 token 数量比代码少得多，所以你的实际体验可能会有所不同。
但大致来说，100-200tok/s 对我来说已经相当快了。低于 50tok/s 的输出会让人感觉越来越慢。讽刺的是，超过 200tok/s 似乎反而让人有些不安——你可以在这里试试 10,000tok/s+ (!) 的模型。我确信，随着我们逐渐习惯这种速度并推动智能体处理更复杂的工作，这种感觉的阈值也会逐渐提高。
鉴于我认为有许多新模型已经达到了前述标准——例如 GLM5.2 和 DeepSeek V4 Flash GA——它们是开放权重且体积较小，我们现在拥有了丰富的模型和速度选择。如果你查看 OpenRouter 上各个提供商对 GLM5.2 的速度排名，你会发现服务速度的跨度极大——从底部的不到 30tok/s 到顶部的 129tok/s。
这是开放权重生态系统的另一个巨大优势。虽然成本上的好处显而易见，但提供商们同样有动力在速度上展开竞争，这确实非常有趣。[3]
但也存在局限性
如果你熟悉帕累托法则和阿姆达尔定律，你就会知道接下来会发生什么。
假设“足够好”的模型继续变得越来越快，那么速度优势将越来越多地消耗在工具调用以及我们人类对它们的监督上。
假设有一个使用处理速度为 50tok/s 的模型的智能体。大部分时间都花在等待推理返回上。现在以 250tok/s 的速度运行同一轮次，你会发现越来越明显的是，瓶颈转移到了“本地”机器上的工具调用以及你的决策过程上。
数字是粗略的，但整体趋势成立。模型速度提升 5 倍只能让单轮次速度提升 2 倍，因为另外那 25 秒并没有缩短。
更糟糕的是，在这些工具调用上提升本地机器的速度正陷入停滞，因为 AI 导致硬件成本呈抛物线般飙升。这又是 AI 市场带来的另一个奇怪的衍生效应。
因此我怀疑（至少目前是这样），对速度的需求在越过某个临界点后是有限的。毫无疑问，在某些场景下海量的推理是有用的（比如数学研究），加快推理速度也会有所帮助。但我预计许多智能体将开始在本地/内部硬件、数据库调用以及其他延迟上遇到瓶颈。
价格战即将打响
有趣的是，OpenAI 在 DeepSeek V4 Flash 正式发布前夕将其 Luna 变体的成本降低了 80%，使其作为一款前沿模型变得异常实惠。虽然与 GLM5.2 相比，我并没有从它那里获得出色输出的好运，但我认为这预示着这一端的市场将出现一场绝对的价格血战。
你可以在 OpenRouter 上的 GLM5.2 看到这种情况——不断提供折扣以试图吸引客户。GLM5.2 的价格已经降到了 $0.42/$1.32/MTok——仅为 Opus 价格的 5%。
虽然最便宜的选项速度很慢，但只需多花一点点钱，你就可以从 DeepInfra 获得 109tok/s 的速度。
随着下一代 GPU 在未来几个月内开始部署——包括 Nvidia 的 Vera Rubin 系列和 AMD 的 MI400s 等——这些芯片中的新 HBM4 内存仅凭内存带宽就能在输出 token 上带来 2 倍以上的速度提升，再加上额外的计算和互连，提升还会更多。
到了 2027 年，我们很有可能拥有质量极高、价格合理且运行速度超过 500tok/s 的模型。一天中大部分时间都盯着“仍在以极高算力思考”的状态，可能终于要成为历史了。
值得关注的一件趣事——我也不确定该押注哪一边——是那些庞大的 2-3T+ 参数模型在日常任务中是否真的表现得显著更好。一方面，感觉我们现在已经达到了一个最佳平衡点；另一方面，模型中多出一个数量级的智能可能会让这个平衡点显得非常、非常原始。
其次当然是没完没了的安全护栏触发，这往往发生在最糟糕的时候——正当我深入一项困难任务，觉得我正需要 Fable 提供的额外“火力”时，但这又是另一回事了。 ↩︎
一个经典的例子是 Craigslist 或 Hacker News 这样的网站。虽然它们看起来过时了，但响应速度快得惊人，以至于你根本注意不到。同样，你那些“标准”的 SPA 应用为了渲染一个首页要加载 30MB 的 React，大部分时间用起来就像在糖浆里跋涉一样费劲，尽管它们在设计上和产品上肯定投入了巨大的开销。 ↩︎
我知道 OpenAI 和 Anthropic 很久以前就提供过模型的快速变体，但它们的 API 定价令人咋舌。除非你拿着空头支票在基准测试中疯狂刷 token，否则我还没见过谁在日常运营中使用它们。拥有价格合理且速度超快的优秀模型，是最近才加入市场的。 ↩︎

blocks.text: 1st August 2026 - Link Blog

Ten advances in mathematics and theoretical computer science (via) A few days ago it was Anthropic discovering cryptographic weaknesses with Claude using Mythos Preview, spending $100,000 on tokens and with prompts that included "again we are not looking for low hanging fruit, we want proper research to find genuinly hard findings."

Now it's OpenAI's turn to flex. They set "an internal version of Astra, our next major model" on finding solutions to ten mathematical problems that "have seen no progress on the main result for at least a decade". They claim to have spent less than $2,000 at GPT-5.6 Sol token prices on each one.
(No news on how many problems they spent $2,000 on without reaching a solution though.)

The openai/ten-proofs repository has Lean 4 formalizations of their results, and there's also a paper describing the solutions and an additional LLM-generated PDF where the model "reconstructs how the proof came together" based on the unpublished reasoning traces.
That's a decent level of transparency, but I want to see the prompts they used!

A lot of mathematicians online are experiencing a collective burst of Deep Blue. Mathematician Kirwin Hampshire published an impassioned essay last week, The Dark Night of Mathematics, describing "a profound spiritual crisis" brought on by previous (and less significant) results.
OpenAI's results reminds me of what Terence Tao described as "big mathematics" in IEEE Spectrum in June:

Unlike some of his peers, Tao is neither dismissive of AI nor fearful. Instead, he sees it as the catalyst for a fundamental shift in the discipline—a transition toward what he calls “big mathematics.” He envisions a future of large-scale, decentralized collaborations between humans and machines, where complex mathematical tasks can be diced and sliced, with humans claiming the creative parts and AI doing the lion’s share of the technical grunt work.

translations: 2026年8月1日 - 链接博客
数学与理论计算机科学的十项进展（via）几天前，Anthropic 使用 Mythos Preview 让 Claude 发现了密码学弱点，花费了 10 万美元的 token，提示词中包括“再次强调，我们不是在寻找容易摘的果子，我们希望进行真正的研究，以发现真正困难的成果。”
现在轮到 OpenAI 大显身手了。他们让“我们的下一个主要模型 Astra 的内部版本”去寻找十个数学问题的解决方案，这些问题“在主要结果上至少十年没有取得进展”。他们声称，按照 GPT-5.6 Sol 的 token 价格，每个问题花费不到 2000 美元。
（不过，关于他们在多少个问题上花了 2000 美元却未能找到解决方案，目前还没有消息。）
openai/ten-proofs 仓库中有他们结果的 Lean 4 形式化证明，还有一篇描述这些解决方案的论文，以及一份由 LLM 生成的 PDF，模型在其中基于未公开的推理轨迹“重构了证明是如何完成的”。
这种透明度还算不错，但我还是想看看他们使用的提示词！
网上许多数学家正在集体经历 Deep Blue 时刻。数学家 Kirwin Hampshire 上周发表了一篇慷慨激昂的文章《数学的至暗时刻》，描述了由之前（且不那么重要的）成果引发的“一场深刻的精神危机”。
OpenAI 的成果让我想起了 Terence Tao 在 6 月份的 IEEE Spectrum 中所描述的“大数学”：
与他的一些同行不同，Tao 既不轻视 AI，也不惧怕它。相反，他将其视为该学科发生根本性转变的催化剂——向他所称的“大数学”过渡。他设想了一个未来：人类与机器之间进行大规模、去中心化的协作，复杂的数学任务可以被切分，人类负责创造性部分，而 AI 则承担绝大部分技术性的繁重工作。

articles.title: Giving and taking credit in big tech companies
articles.titleZh: Giving and taking credit in big tech companies
articles.summary: Giving and taking credit in big tech companies

blocks.text: Engineers often complain that visibility should be their manager’s job. In other words, they think engineers should be able to focus on the code, while their manager figures out who’s doing well and rewards them.

This attitude is an extension of the “school fantasy”: the idea that your workplace should operate by the same rules as your school or university. After all, you didn’t have to worry about “visibility” during your education. You simply did the assignments and tests you were given, and if you did well you were rewarded with a good grade.

Many big tech companies encourage this attitude, because it helps them recruit smart graduates. They fashion their workplaces to look and feel like a university, even calling the physical space “campuses”. But it’s still work, not school. If you treat it like school, you are going to have a bad time.
Taking credit

The first lesson many new engineers learn is that you have to take credit for your work. If you silently jump in to help a struggling project and get it back on track, there’s no guarantee of reward. Credit will naturally flow to the project lead, not you. In fact, if this project is outside of your direct team, it’s likely you will be punished for it: to your manager, it will look like you’re simply doing nothing at all.

Even when your manager is watching your work, credit is largely uncorrelated with how well you did. That’s because, unlike at school, you are the subject-matter expert on your own work. Software systems are so complicated that only the people who work on them can hope to understand them, and even that understanding is always imperfect. If even experts can’t reliably estimate the difficulty of changes, how is your manager supposed to assess your technical performance? The answer is they aren’t. They’re simply not qualified to assess it.

Instead, smart managers will find engineers on your team they trust and ask them how you’re doing. On small teams that have worked on a single codebase for a long time, this works okay, because everyone’s familiar enough to judge everyone else’s work. On large teams with a high rate of codebase churn, it goes badly, since they’re just guessing. On teams with a nasty, cutthroat culture, it sometimes goes very badly, since this is a good opportunity to actively sabotage the engineers who might threaten you.

Experienced engineers know how to take the credit themselves. When they do something good, they tell their manager about it. They write internal posts explaining why it was technically difficult and how they solved it (the audience for these is partially those trusted engineers, and partially the managers who will see a long technical post and think “wow!” without reading it). They actively build trust with their management chain. Worrying about this stuff is the beginning of playing politics.
Giving credit

There’s a kind of engineer who’s learned how to take credit but hasn’t learned any other lessons yet. They’re proactive about telling people what they’ve done, and they always maintain a “brag doc”. In particular, they love to talk about the parts they did by themselves, since those are least vulnerable to other people coming in to claim credit. You can tell they’re jealously guarding whatever credit they’ve managed to accumulate. The lesson this kind of engineer hasn’t learned is that you can often accumulate credit best by giving it away.

To see why, consider how credit flows up inside a tech company. I wrote above that your manager can’t assess the quality of your technical work on their own, but instead has to rely on other engineers they trust. They’ll quietly ask those engineers “hey, was this project really that impressive?“. In fact, often there are multiple layers of this at play1. In big companies, line managers usually don’t decide who gets promoted or who gets a raise: they make recommendations to their manager, who has their own network of trusted engineers (confusingly, sometimes these networks overlap). The point is that there is a large group of people behind the scenes who will quietly and informally judge the value of your work.

Succeeding at a tech company is largely about finding ways to get these people on your side. The easiest way is to share your credit with them — and since you don’t know who exactly is in this group, you should be sharing your credit freely. When you get feedback from other engineers, publicly thank them and mention them in your internal posts about the project. Find opportunities to ask for small favors, so you have an excuse to give other people credit. As best you can, make your individual projects at least partially group projects.

Sharing credit with others gives them a reason to support you. A shared project you’ve worked on reflects well on everybody: on you, for working well with others, on the people you’ve worked with, for the same reason, and for your manager, for fostering such a great environment of cooperation. Lots of people have good reason to talk that project up, because it’s partly their project too. On the other hand, a project you’ve jealously kept to yourself reflects well on nobody: you come across as antisocial and your peers come across as unhelpful.
Blame

Blame operates by the same rules as credit. When something goes badly wrong, managers will ask their networks “hey, who screwed up here?” The answer to this question is never simple. Even on a purely technical level, failures always involve an interaction between multiple complex systems, any one of which could conceivably have been built so as to avoid the failure. In other words, competent engineers can assign blame pretty much wherever they want.

Because of this, it’s risky to have a project for which you’re clearly the only one getting credit. When something goes wrong, the network of people who will assign blame will likely be implicated in every part of the system but yours. They will be incentivized to attribute fault to the brand-new thing that they don’t understand and are not responsible for. If instead that network had been involved in your project — if they’d been in a position to share the credit — they’d be less incentivized to blame it.

Of course, engineers are (mostly) not scheming viziers who make purely self-interested decisions. When asked who to blame, they usually make a good-faith effort to answer honestly. But in an area where there’s no single clear right answer, it’s human nature to be at least a little bit guided by your incentives. Nobody likes to think they’re responsible for a group failure.
Conclusion

Credit and blame are the currencies of tech companies (and often directly translate to the actual amount of currency you get to take home). For technical roles, managers assign credit and blame based on lots of quiet conversations with their trusted engineers. This can be a rude awakening for very junior engineers who are used to having their work assessed by an expert grader (or less junior engineers who haven’t yet shaken that mindset completely).

Don’t expect to get credit simply by putting your head down and doing good work. You have to find some way to tell people what you’re doing and why it’s important: internal blog posts, mentioning it in 1:1s with your manager, or anything else you can think of. But don’t take self-promotion too far. It’s a bad idea to try and hoard all the credit for your projects, for two reasons.

First, sharing credit with other people gives them a reason to talk positively about your project. Credit is not a zero-sum game: if you do it right, you can get other people to build up your credit for you. Second, hoarding credit sets yourself up as a lightning rod for blame. Projects where the credit is concentrated in one or two people are automatically2 blamed for complex problems, because nobody is incentivized to defend them.

This is a classic example of an illegible-but-essential part of a software company. I wrote about this general phenomenon in Seeing like a software company.
↩

Of course, if you do really screw up, you’ll be blamed no matter what. I’m talking here about complex failures where it’s non-trivial to attribute blame to a single source.

translations: 工程师们经常抱怨说，提高可见度应该是他们经理的工作。换句话说，他们认为工程师应该能够专注于代码，而由经理来弄清楚谁做得好并给予奖励。
这种态度是“学校幻想”的延伸：即认为你的工作场所应该按照与你的中小学或大学相同的规则来运转。毕竟，在求学期间你不需要担心“可见度”。你只需完成布置的作业和考试，如果你做得好，就会得到一个好成绩作为奖励。
许多大型科技公司鼓励这种态度，因为这有助于他们招募聪明的毕业生。他们把工作场所打造得看起来和感觉上都像一所大学，甚至把物理空间称为“校园”。但这仍然是工作，不是学校。如果你把它当成学校，你会吃大亏的。
获取认可
许多新工程师学到的第一课是，你必须为自己的工作争取认可。如果你默默地介入帮助一个陷入困境的项目并使其重回正轨，并不能保证会得到奖励。功劳自然会归功于项目负责人，而不是你。事实上，如果这个项目不在你的直属团队范围内，你甚至可能会因此受到惩罚：在你的经理看来，你似乎什么都没做。
即使你的经理在关注你的工作，认可度在很大程度上也与你做得好坏无关。这是因为，与学校不同，你是自己工作领域的专家。软件系统非常复杂，只有从事这些系统工作的人才有希望理解它们，而且即使是这种理解也总是不完美的。如果连专家都无法可靠地评估变更的难度，你的经理又该如何评估你的技术表现呢？答案是他们做不到。他们根本没有资格去评估。
相反，聪明的经理会在你的团队中找到他们信任的工程师，并询问他们你做得怎么样。在长期使用单一代码库的小团队中，这种方法效果还不错，因为每个人都足够熟悉，可以评判彼此的工作。在代码库变动率很高的大团队中，这种方法效果很差，因为他们只是在猜测。在文化恶劣、竞争激烈的团队中，这种方法有时会非常糟糕，因为这是一个主动破坏可能威胁到你的工程师的好机会。
经验丰富的工程师知道如何为自己争取认可。当他们做出成绩时，他们会告诉经理。他们会写内部文章解释为什么这在技术上很困难以及他们是如何解决的（这些文章的受众部分是那些受信任的工程师，部分是那些看到长篇技术文章就会不读内容而直接觉得“哇！”的经理）。他们积极与自己的管理链建立信任。操心这些事情就是玩弄职场政治的开端。
给予认可
有一种工程师学会了如何获取认可，但还没有学到其他任何经验。他们主动告诉别人自己做了什么，并且总是维护一份“自夸文档”。特别是，他们喜欢谈论自己独立完成的部分，因为这些部分最不容易被别人插手抢功。你可以看出他们在小心翼翼地守护着自己设法积累的任何功劳。这种工程师还没有学到的一课是，你通常可以通过把功劳让给别人来最好地积累自己的功劳。

要明白其中的原因，不妨想想科技公司内部功劳是如何向上传递的。我在上文提到过，你的直属经理无法独自评估你技术工作的质量，而是必须依赖他们信任的其他工程师。他们会私下询问这些工程师：“嘿，这个项目真的有那么出色吗？”事实上，这种情况往往涉及多个层级。在大公司里，一线经理通常不直接决定谁升职或谁加薪：他们会向自己的经理提出建议，而那位经理也有自己信任的工程师网络（令人困惑的是，有时这些网络是重叠的）。关键在于，有一大群人在幕后会私下且非正式地评判你工作的价值。
在科技公司取得成功，很大程度上在于想办法让这些人站在你这边。最简单的方法就是与他们分享你的功劳——既然你不知道这个群体里到底有谁，你就应该大方地分享你的功劳。当你收到其他工程师的反馈时，公开感谢他们，并在你关于该项目的内部帖子中提及他们。寻找机会请别人帮点小忙，这样你就有借口把功劳分给别人。尽你所能，让你的个人项目至少部分成为团队项目。
与他人分享功劳给了他们支持你的理由。你参与的一个共享项目能让每个人都面上有光：对你来说，是因为你与他人合作良好；对与你合作的人来说，也是出于同样的原因；对你的经理来说，则是因为他营造了如此出色的合作环境。很多人都有充分的理由去称赞那个项目，因为那在一定程度上也是他们的项目。另一方面，一个你小心翼翼据为己有的项目对谁都没有好处：你会显得不合群，而你的同事也会显得不乐于助人。
责任
责任的归属遵循与功劳相同的规则。当出现严重问题时，经理们会询问他们的人脉网络：“嘿，这里是谁搞砸了？”这个问题的答案从来都不简单。即使在纯技术层面上，故障也总是涉及多个复杂系统之间的相互作用，其中任何一个系统在理论上都可以通过某种构建方式来避免该故障。换句话说，有能力的工程师几乎可以把责任推给他们想推的任何地方。
正因如此，如果有一个项目明显只有你一个人获得功劳，那是很危险的。当出现问题时，负责归咎责任的人脉网络可能会牵涉到系统中除了你之外的所有部分。他们会受到利益驱使，将过错归咎于他们不理解且不负责的那个全新事物。相反，如果那个网络参与了你的项目——如果他们处于可以分享功劳的位置——他们归咎责任的动机就会小得多。
当然，工程师（在大多数情况下）并不是那种只做纯粹利己决定的阴谋家。当被问及该怪谁时，他们通常会出于善意努力如实回答。但在没有单一明确正确答案的领域，至少受到一点自身利益的驱使是人的天性。没有人喜欢认为自己要对团队的失败负责。
结论
功劳和过失是科技公司的流通货币（而且通常直接转化为你能带回家的实际货币金额）。对于技术岗位，管理者会通过与信任的工程师进行大量私下交流来分配功劳和过失。这对于习惯了由专家评分来评估自己工作的初级工程师来说，可能是一次令人猛醒的教训（对于那些还没有完全摆脱这种心态的较资深工程师也是如此）。
不要指望仅仅埋头苦干就能获得功劳。你必须找到某种方式告诉别人你在做什么以及为什么这很重要：内部博客文章、在与经理的 1:1 会议中提及，或者你能想到的任何其他方式。但不要把自我推销做得太过火。试图独揽项目的所有功劳是个坏主意，原因有两个。
首先，与他人分享功劳会给他们一个积极评价你项目的理由。功劳不是零和博弈：如果你做得对，你可以让别人为你积累功劳。其次，囤积功劳会让你成为承担过失的避雷针。功劳集中在一两个人身上的项目，在遇到复杂问题时会自然而然地受到指责，因为没有人有动力去为它们辩护。

这是软件公司中难以言明但至关重要的部分的典型例子。我在《像软件公司一样观察》（Seeing like a software company）一文中写过这个普遍现象。
↩

当然，如果你真的搞砸了，无论如何你都会受到指责。我在这里谈论的是那些很难将过失归咎于单一来源的复杂失败。

blocks.text:
Yesterday, OpenAI announced the solution to ten open problems in
mathematics, all discovered by a yet-unreleased model. There’s only one, the
coding theory one, where I know enough to say “huh, that’s important”, but
according to the mathematicians I trust this is important.

Inevitably, people will spin some sophistry to cope, to convince themselves
nothing will change. And that’s fine. People need to cope. But we can’t put our
heads in the sand forever while the world is transformed around us. So, here is
a list of ways people will cope about AI taking over mathematics, and how each
cope is likely to be refuted by reality.

My intent is not to horribly depress everyone but rather to help them metabolize
the implications of this technology. The arguments here are somewhat portable:
replace “mathematics” with “botany” or whatever as needed.
Moving the goalposts.
Obvious and not worth addressing.

“We will direct the AIs, point them at problems and research areas
to solve.”

The AIs will exceed humans in taste and intuition. At some point, the
human pointing the way will get worse results than the human saying “here’s a
proof checker, have fun” and paying for the tokens.
“We will teach the mathematics AI discovers.”

The AIs will be better teachers than the humans. In any case, there won’t be a
human audience for expository work of frontier math.
“We will choose how to canonize the results AI discovers.”

This is a nice cope. The AIs are explorers out in the frontiers, the humans
gratefully receive their Lean proofs, and then discourse over them, choose which
results are relevant, shape those results into a little brick for the great
cathedral of algebra. Analogous to the above: the AIs will build the
cathedral on their own. They will be better architects than us.
“We will become students of AI mathematics.”

This works until the AIs have blasted so deep into the deductive closure of
mathlib that the distance from elementary mathematics to the frontier exceeds
what any human can hope to learn in their lifetime, no matter how narrow their
focus.
“We need humans to understand the results AI discovers.”

We won’t! This misunderstands who the audience will be. AIs will do frontier
math, downstream, AIs will use the new math to do frontier science, finally, AIs
will use the new science to do frontier engineering. No human needs to
understand any of it, firms that put humans in the loop to understand the
results will be outcompeted by those which don’t.

The result is that we will live in a demon-haunted world, full of marvelous
devices whose operation we will not understand, based on engineering principles
we will not understand, discovered using formalisms we will not understand.
“Computers are already superhuman at chess, yet we still play chess.”

Unlike most copes, I think this one is interesting. Computers are superhuman
chess players, yet we don’t care, and continue playing as normal. Why should
mathematics be different?

The main reason, I think, is that chess is self-contained: results from chess
don’t help us understand the orbits of the planets or the binding of drugs to
protein surfaces. But mathematics, famously, is the great dynamo of
science, the best language and method for understanding the world. A machine
that can replace a human mathematician, but better and faster and cheaper, is
materially useful; a better chess engine is not.

If two computers which are superhuman at chess play against each other, who
cares? There is little demand for this, so there is no-one to outcompete. A
superhuman mathematician is different.

“Mathematics will change, but mathematicians and the mathematically-inclined
will still do math on their own.”

I think this ignores that mathematics is embedded in a social context. As an
example: when it became clear that AI would eat software, my cope was: “I’m
perfectly happy to become an engineering manager to agents in my professional
life; in my off time, I can still write code for the pleasure of it.”

And I do. But this cope ignores the effect AI has had on the social context of
writing code: the discourse has gotten worse, and vastly more anti-intellectual;
people who used to talk about type systems and compilers now talk about “loops”
and “harnesses”; you put a hand-created project on GitHub and you get slop PRs;
you open a link to an interesting-looking project and find the README is
unreadable AI slop. And in the long-term, it is demoralizing to ponder: will
anyone design a new programming language? Dually, if I design a new language,
will anyone care? If I write a library that introduces an elegant new formalism
to solve a particular problem, will anyone use it?

Which is to say: no man is an island. You can do mathematics on your own, but
you’ll find that very, very few people can sustain any activity long-term on the
basis of intrinsic motivation alone. We are social animals: we care about being
useful, about status, about outcomes in the world.
Conclusion

I think I should end on a cheerful note. So let me try. Personally, I don’t
believe technology is inevitable. “Inevitable” is a word reserved for the orbits
of the planets. Nothing that is the product of human action is inevitable. We
can choose to obsolete ourselves, and we can choose not to. We can realize that
AGI is a devil’s bargain: we may accelerate technical progress, we may
unlock all kinds of wonderful tech tree nodes like life extension earlier than
we would otherwise; but the result, in the long run, is that humans become, at
best, like pets under the care of vastly more powerful entities.
A Note On Prediction

The future is not certain, but I’ve phrased everything above as definitive for
simplicity. If we take the possibility of AGI and ASI seriously, if AI continues
to progress as it has for the past ~6 years, I think this is a reasonable view
of where things will go.

Probably the best argument against AI progress is “RL doesn’t generalize well,
we have seen immense progress in verifiable domains like formalized mathematics
and coding, we will see less progress in domains that are intuitive or
unformalizable”. Maybe true. But billions of dollars and thousands of very smart
people—and, increasingly, very smart models—are being thrown at this
problem. How long does this cope last?

显而易见，不值得讨论。
“我们将指导 AI，将它们指向需要解决的问题和研究领域。”
AI 在品味和直觉上将超越人类。在某个时刻，指明方向的人类所获得的结果，会比那些说“这是一个证明检查器，玩得开心”并为 token 付费的人类更差。
“我们将教授 AI 发现的数学。”
AI 会比人类成为更好的老师。无论如何，前沿数学的解说性工作将不再有人类受众。
“我们将选择如何将 AI 发现的结果奉为经典。”
这是一个不错的应对方式。AI 是前沿的探索者，人类感激地接收它们的 Lean 证明，然后对它们进行论述，选择哪些结果是相关的，将这些结果塑造成代数大教堂的一块小砖头。与上述情况类似：AI 会自己建造大教堂。它们会是比我们更好的建筑师。
“我们将成为 AI 数学的学生。”
这招在 AI 深入探索 mathlib 的演绎闭包之前是管用的，一旦深入到从基础数学到前沿的距离超过了任何人类在有生之年所能学到的极限，无论他们的专注点多么狭窄，这招就失效了。
“我们需要人类来理解 AI 发现的结果。”
我们不需要！这误解了受众是谁。AI 将从事前沿数学研究，在下游，AI 将利用新的数学进行前沿科学研究，最后，AI 将利用新的科学进行前沿工程开发。没有任何人类需要理解其中的任何内容，将人类置于循环中以理解结果的公司，将被那些不这么做的公司击败。
结果是我们将生活在一个群魔乱舞的世界里，充满了奇妙的设备，我们不了解它们的运作方式，它们基于我们不了解的工程原理，使用我们不了解的形式体系被发现。
“计算机在国际象棋上已经超越人类了，但我们仍然在下国际象棋。”
与大多数应对方式不同，我认为这个很有趣。计算机是超人类的国际象棋棋手，但我们不在乎，并继续像往常一样下棋。为什么数学会有所不同？
我认为主要原因是，国际象棋是自成一体的：国际象棋的结果不能帮助我们理解行星的轨道或药物与蛋白质表面的结合。但众所周知，数学是科学的巨大发电机，是理解世界的最佳语言和方法。一台能够取代人类数学家，而且更好、更快、更便宜的机器，在物质上是有用的；而一个更好的国际象棋引擎则不然。
如果两个在国际象棋上超越人类的计算机互相对弈，谁会在乎呢？这种需求微乎其微，因此也没有人可以去竞争。但超越人类的数学家则不同。
“数学将会改变，但数学家和具有数学倾向的人仍然会自己做数学。”
我认为这忽略了数学是嵌入在社会语境中的。举个例子：当 AI 将吞噬软件行业变得显而易见时，我的应对方式是：“在职业生涯中，我非常乐意成为智能体的工程经理；在业余时间，我仍然可以为了乐趣而写代码。”

我确实这么做了。但这种应对方式忽略了 AI 对编写代码的社会语境所产生的影响：讨论变得更糟，而且反智得多；过去谈论类型系统和编译器的人现在谈论的是“循环”和“测试套件”；你把一个手工制作的项目放在 GitHub 上，却收到一堆垃圾 PR；你打开一个看起来很有趣的项目链接，却发现 README 是无法阅读的 AI 垃圾。从长远来看，思考这些问题令人沮丧：还会有人设计新的编程语言吗？反之，如果我设计了一种新语言，会有人在乎吗？如果我写了一个引入优雅的新形式化方法来解决特定问题的库，会有人使用它吗？
也就是说：没有人是一座孤岛。你可以自己做数学，但你会发现，很少有人能仅凭内在动机长期维持任何活动。我们是社会动物：我们在乎是否有用，在乎地位，在乎世界上的结果。
结论
我想我应该以一个乐观的基调结束。所以让我试试。就我个人而言，我不相信技术是不可避免的。“不可避免”这个词是留给行星轨道的。任何人类行动的产物都不是不可避免的。我们可以选择淘汰自己，也可以选择不这么做。我们可以认识到 AGI 是一种魔鬼的交易：我们可能会加速技术进步，可能会比原本更早解锁诸如寿命延长等各种奇妙的科技树节点；但长远来看，其结果是，人类充其量只会变成在强大得多的实体照顾下的宠物。
关于预测的说明
未来是不确定的，但为了简单起见，我把上面的一切都表述为确定性的。如果我们认真对待 AGI 和 ASI 的可能性，如果 AI 继续像过去大约 6 年那样发展，我认为这是对事物走向的一个合理看法。
反对 AI 进步的最佳论点可能是“RL 的泛化能力不强，我们在形式化数学和编程等可验证领域看到了巨大的进步，但在直觉性或无法形式化的领域，我们将看到较少的进步”。也许是对的。但数十亿美元和成千上万非常聪明的人——以及越来越多非常聪明的模型——正在被投入到这个问题中。这种应对方式还能持续多久？

blocks.text: Second order linear differential equations with polynomial coefficients form their own area of study. This seems like a narrow class of equations, but it’s very important in applications.

This class of equations seems like a mathematically natural topic, but why is it so important in applications? I did a PhD in differential equations without ever learning why. The theory of second order linear equations with polynomial coefficients is too complicated for undergraduate courses [0] and too well-established for graduate courses [1].

The explanation that I was missing can be found in the first chapter of [2]. The PDEs that are common in physics are separable in various coordinate systems, meaning that in these coordinate systems the PDEs reduce to ODEs. These ODEs either have polynomial coefficients, or there is a change of variables which makes the ODEs have polynomial coefficients.
See this writeup that looks at the Helmholtz and Laplace equations in 11 coordinate systems.
[0] You may see the simplest parts of the theory in a section on solving ODEs with power series. But textbooks don’t go very far for good reasons.

[1] Unfortunately, a lot of really useful topics are left out of the graduate curriculum because they’re too well understood to provide thesis topics. Or the problems that are still open have been open for so long that they’re likely too hard to be cracked by a graduate student.
[2] Gerhard Kristensson. Second Order Differential Equations: Special Functions and their Classification. Springer, 2010.

articles.titleZh: 贴上标签：定价枪与条形码的历史博弈
articles.summary: 定价枪本应在条形码普及前就被淘汰，但各州的法律将其作为抵御条形码这一“可怕技术”的保护伞而人为保留。条形码技术在早期面临着法律层面的阻力和消费者对透明定价的担忧。州立法者通过强制要求商品明码标价，使得定价枪在零售业中得以苟延残喘。随着零售业的全面现代化和条形码系统的成熟，定价枪最终才彻底退出历史舞台。这段历史揭示了技术更替背后鲜为人知的政策与法律博弈。
articles.summaryEn: The pricing gun should have been obsolete long before it actually was, but state laws artificially kept it alive as a shield against the intimidating barcode. Early barcode technology faced legal resistance and consumer concerns about transparent pricing. By mandating clearly marked prices on individual items, state legislators allowed pricing guns to linger in the retail industry. Only with the full modernization of retail and the maturation of barcode systems did pricing guns finally exit the historical stage. This history reveals the hidden policy and legal struggles behind technological replacement.

blocks.text: Today in Tedium: Determining how much something costs shouldn’t be difficult, but in an ecosystem where everything is driven by highly personalized data, concerns are rising that prices might not be on stable ground. Recently, some states and regulators have started to scrutinize e-paper price tags out of a concern that those tags will enable pricing that adapts to demand—or worse, to the customer. A major union, the United Food and Commercial Workers International Union (UFCW), even announced plans to launch a campaign against electronic shelf labels, as they’re called. But what if I were to tell you that this concern is not in fact a new one, and it more or less played out like this 50 years ago, on a technology that most people take for granted today? That’s right, we’re talking about barcodes, along with its predecessor technology, the pricing gun. Today’s Tedium dives into the surprisingly long-running conflict between price tags and barcodes. — Ernie @ Tedium

The number of pricing guns that Sears used during a 1989 promotion that saw the company permanently lower prices at its stores throughout the United States. (The company also used 100 million pricing labels, which is about the amount, in dollars, that the retailer spent on the campaign.) The moment was big and showy, and involved the company closing its stores for 42 hours, with a single store having to mark down prices on about 1 million individual items.
The pricing gun: Where the hell did it come from?

It turns out that searching for something called a “pricing gun” is kind of tough to do. As our search engines have declined, anything with the word “gun” on it is suspect, even if it’s for something fairly innocuous.

But the pricing gun is nonetheless an excellent example of a device that has helped millions of people identify shifting prices, yet is only truly used in one context: Retail. You can clearly see the roots of where it came from by taking separate, unrelated ideas and combining them. You can look at things like combination locks, typewriters, and rubber stamps, and see how they were combined in novel ways to produce an iconic piece of supermarket kit.

In many ways, the pricing gun, which at its root takes a sticker with self-stick adhesive, prints a price on it, and tags it on a product, is a synthesis of multiple ideas that, together, created something new. We talked about one, self-stick adhesive (terrible name upon its initial release BTW), six years ago. Great innovation by the adhesive giant now known as Avery Dennison, but not one that was designed to scale. Imagine putting a label on every single product in a grocery store, by hand, writing the prices out, cutting the stickers, and so on. It would be the definition of Tedium.

But there were other lanes for price labeling that were already starting to emerge. Consider the printing process, for example, which essentially involved pressing metal or rubberized content onto ink, then taking the ink-stained surface and pressing it onto a sheet of paper. These were once parts of giant machines, but they could also be made handheld or somewhat more portable. The first commercial typewriter, the Hansen Writing Ball, feels like it could’ve been used for price tags if put in a slightly different context. All of this fed into the idea of the handheld “rubber stamp,” which gradually gained a “self-inking” capability, which meant that you didn’t even need an inkwell to dip them in.

Meanwhile, innovations in the combination lock during the 1870s began to bleed to similar tools. If you make the numbers on a combination lock lean outward rather than inward, the wheels could be used not unlike a printing press. So you can see where this is going!

All of this led to the Bates Automatic Numbering Machine, a press-down device Edwin G. Bates patented around 1901. While intended for checks and similar documents, the approach is fairly similar to how a price tagger works. You set the number, you press down on the page, and then it goes to the next number for the next page. This device helped to reshape the legal industry in particular, as pages could now easily be numbered, and became known enough that “Bates numbering” became a common business-world shorthand. In fact, some later versions of the device could keep the same number for multiple stamps.

This was clearly the path that led to adjustable price tagging, though other inventors took the helm. At the turn of the 20th century, Frederick Kohnle of the Automatic Pin Ticketing Machine Company effectively brought this process to price tags of the kind that might be attached to clothing, rather than to stickers. (It wasn’t quite handheld, but you can see the DNA bleed through.)
Another inventor working in the same area, William G. Metcalf, developed a pricing ticket machine, and as The Price Gun Store notes, the patents ultimately came under Kohnle’s ownership.

Kohnle has a lot of patent filings to his name around pricing tagging technology, so while he didn’t necessarily create the pricing gun, he likely created the environment that led to its eventual creation. His innovations live through to the modern day in another company he founded, Monarch Tag and Label—which is, of course, now owned by Avery Dennison and specializes in pricing guns.

Monarch, which also spent time as a subsidiary of Pitney Bowes, developed one of the most important direct predecessors to the modern pricing gun, the “Dial-A-Pricer,” in the 1950s. But it wasn’t the only one. As the 2023 book Fixing Prices: A Century of Setting, Posting and Adjusting Retail Prices notes, a number of related solutions started to emerge around the same period, most notably the Garvey price stamper, invented by Ed Garvey in the 1950s.

What’s interesting is that Google Patents appears to have a full-on example of a pricing gun patent filed in the 1940s, predating Monarch’s own gun-shaped attempts. But there’s no evidence that the device, developed by Robert S. Kafka for the Midland Equipment Corp., ever meaningfully made it to market—literally no information about the invention, beyond a defunct-company listing in the Robert D. Fisher Manual of Valuable and Worthless Securities, exists beyond the patent. Other companies eventually developed their own versions, including Monarch and Garvey, along with the Japanese company SATO.
But Kafka’s innovation is definitely worth our time, as it diagnoses the problem thoughtfully:

In stores, and particularly in stores where large numbers of articles are to be price-tagged, the labor of affixing the price tags is very great. For instance, if 1,000 glasses are to be labelled “$.39,” it is necessary to take a thousand labels, write, print, or type the price upon each one, after which the operator is required to separate the protective backing tape from the adhesive side of the label and apply the label to the glass. This entire operation is done by hand. The complexity of the operation is immeasurably increased by the number of articles that are to be labelled for sale and by the variety of prices at which the articles are to be sold.It is an object of this invention to make a hand labeller which will print the proper price mark and apply a price label by adhesive to an article.
If you can label a thousand cans just by setting a price and hitting a button, you’ve turned a multi-hour process into something that can be done in a matter of minutes.

If Kafka didn’t commercialize his invention at a large scale, many other companies soon did. Fixing Prices co-authors Franck Cochoy, Johan Hagberg, and Hans Kjellberg credit Monarch for spreading the innovation far and wide:

However, the Monarch company did much more: it paved the way for rebalancing prices and qualities on item labels, reunifying the scattered languages of manufactured qualities (on product packaging) and retail prices (on store shelves), and thus reagencing product labeling in favor of the grocers. This development took several decades and relied on a number of innovations to come fully into fruition, along a complex process of qualitization, digitalization, and paperization of shelf labels.

Let’s think about what they wrote for a second: If grocers can label devices by the hundreds in a matter of minutes, that means they can raise or lower prices much more quickly than they could before. It’s not quite automation; someone has to put their mark on all those cans or pairs of pants. But you can put a price label on top of the other price label and all of a sudden a $2.00 can of food can jump in price to $2.99.

(Plus, it allowed retailers to put their mark on the products, literally. Old price tags, some of which can be seen on Flickr, are often seen as a great way of determining a sealed object’s age and vintage.)

In this light, the barcode, which was printed on the product by the manufacturer rather than the retailer, could be seen as a way to put the product seller back in charge of their MSRP destiny. But oddly, the relatively manual process of price tagging actually became something of a rallying cry for consumers and unions, rather than the retailers or manufacturers.
Which leads us to the 1970s, when retailers attempted to innovate past them.

The estimated number of pricing tags that could be created from a single piece of 8.5-inch by 11-inch sheet of paper. The Anderson Economic Group shared this detail in a 2010 report arguing against a Michigan law that mandated price tagging. (It was clearly part of a larger lobbying effort against the law, and consumer advocates pushed against the report, so take any of its findings with a grain of salt.) The research firm estimated that if one were to combine the paper use of every grocery store in the state just on price tags, it would be a stack of paper nearly as tall as the Empire State Building. And it added that this was actually something of an undercount. “Many price stickers are larger than those used in our calculations, some items end up with multiple price stickers—especially if re-priced—and equally significant amounts of adhesive and ink must also be used to price each item,” the firm wrote. “Account for these factors, and spread the waste over the many smaller retailers within the state, and the numbers magnify greatly.”
How Michigan became ground zero for a price-tag debate

In the late ’90s, as I’ve written many times, I started my first job at a grocery store—and immediately came to hate the bottle machines. Those machines, which attempted to automate bottle deposit laws, were not unique to Michigan but emerged thanks to some unique quirks in state law.

But one thing I did not realize at the time was that Michigan law was also onerous in another way: With pricing. Thanks to state law, my grocery store had to have employees go around the stores and do nothing for hours but put price tags on tens of thousands of items. These items each had to be tagged individually, even though there was a price listing near the original spot on the shelf.
But it’s not like we had phones on us at all times when we could spot check the price, like we do now. So there was a certain logic to it, even if retailers did not like it.
The law, passed in 1976, came about despite the fact that the barcode had emerged at this time. And honestly, it emerged because of it, in part because of union concerns.

“There is an attempt being made to replace clearly marked prices on items with unintelligible lines that can only be deciphered by a computer,” said William C. Marshall, the president of the Michigan State AFL-CIO, in a 1976 wire story. “This would make comparison shopping in the supermarkets impossible and could become the greatest ripoff of consumers imaginable.”

(Other states passed laws too; Massachusetts actually had a “sticker law” on the books a year longer than Michigan did. And many states require shelf labels. But no states required stickers on quite so many things, quite as strictly, for quite as long.)

It’s not hard to see how this in practice helped to protect jobs while also protecting consumers. After all, if each individual item needed to be tagged, that meant someone needed to do the tagging. Any retailer that failed to tag its items was on the hook for an up to $25,000 fine. That was enough to bring in part-time reinforcements.
While pricing guns were quite fast and could tag a lot of prices in a short amount of time, it was still a lot of work that wouldn’t exist if not for this law.

Grocery stores, over the years, grew increasingly opposed to the law, in part because of that labor pressure, which, among other things, required repeated retagging of items as things went on sale or prices naturally increased.
“To individually price those items on a daily basis takes a tremendous amount of labor,” a D&W Food Centers spokesperson told the Grand Rapids Press in 1993.
(Granted, it was a lot less labor than before the pricing gun was a thing, but hey, let them be mad.)

In one wire story, the home improvement retailer Builders Square estimated that one-tenth of the total cost of its labor in the state went to price tagging, a cost of $2.4 million. It was a cost, one that came with added labor concerns, but not ones so significant to, say, ignore the Michigan market.

Despite periodic pressure from grocers, the law didn’t actually get removed from the books until Obama was the president, well after most other states got rid of similar laws. In fact, by the time it did, the pricing gun was more or less of a relic from another time, although one people still saw around from time to time.

There’s a bit of an awkward history to discuss when it comes to a device that looks kind of like a gun, but isn’t one, but is commonly used in retail settings. One of the things I’ve found interesting in my research is that there are many cases out there where a pricing gun was either used as a makeshift weapon, or was mistaken as one.

Obviously, it’s not actually a gun in the Second Amendment sense. It doesn’t fire bullets, it prints prices. But it is large, unwieldy, and kind of looks like a gun from a distance. There are the occasional news stories about a brave employee who successfully shooed away an armed robber with one of these things.

But not every story ends like this. One particularly tragic case, dating to 2010, involved a Texas man named Hayward George Slater Jr., who attempted to rob a convenience store, but reacted negatively to the pricing gun the victim, Prem Sharma, picked up to defend himself. Slater, in an instant, shot and killed Sharma. During his 2011 murder trial, the defense argued that Slater wouldn’t have done anything had the victim not picked up the pricing gun.
(The prosecutor accused the defense of victim-blaming, and as you might assume, the case did not go Slater’s way, even after an appeal.)

Pricing guns over time became a security risk, too. If someone stole a pricing gun that printed the same way as the gun at a local retail store, that meant they could put an extremely low price on a product, defrauding the store. With barcodes, retailers could better control the process, soup to nuts.

Everything I see on Google suggests that pricing guns are extremely niche, and are increasingly uncommon, with only commercial results coming up for these devices. (Hey, maybe this story will change that.) Even crime stories involving pricing guns have slowed down considerably. A big reason for this is that in most of the country, laws mandating price tags went away a long time ago. Which means that the time in the sun for the pricing gun was really, in practice, only about 20 years before the barcode came into play. Which means that the pricing gun was a bridge device with tentacles, thanks to state-level legislation.

Sure, there are newer kinds of devices, such as inkjet printers that can literally print info directly on the box. And labeling itself never went away. But retailers don’t have to use them if they have another way to do so. If the barcode is there, they can just use that.

As hinted at up top, a recent piece from The Food Institute argues that the recent complaints about e-paper price labels and dynamic pricing basically mirror what happened with barcodes 50 years ago. Which means that lobbyists and advocacy groups already know what they’re up against. That had led industry groups like the Food Marketing Institute to argue on their websites that retailers aren’t necessarily surge pricing, but changing prices maybe once a day tops. The only exception? Goods that are reaching their expiration date.

One might argue that the industry has to put the nicest spin on it they possibly can. The fact is, consumers are right to put their guard up, as retailers have not yet proven they can be trusted with the new technology. They more or less earned that trust with barcodes.

Now, to be clear, there may be reasons to use price guns outside of pricing. It might be an effective way of tagging an item’s expiration date, for instance, if it’s suitably small-batch. But we are well past the point where people have to tag prices on every single item every time there’s a change in price.
But you gotta admit, those guns (despite arguably being liabilities, given how often they cropped up in crime blotters) made price tagging as fast as a deeply manual process probably could be.

translations: 今天在 Tedium：确定某件东西的价格本不该是一件难事，但在一个一切由高度个性化数据驱动的生态系统中，人们越来越担心价格可能并不稳定。最近，一些州和监管机构开始审查电子纸价格标签，担心这些标签会实现根据需求——甚至更糟的是，根据顾客——来调整定价。一个主要工会，美国食品与商业工人国际联盟（UFCW），甚至宣布计划发起一场反对电子货架标签（他们这么称呼它）的运动。但如果我告诉你，这种担忧其实并非新鲜事，而且在大约50年前，在一种如今大多数人习以为常的技术上，几乎上演了同样的戏码呢？没错，我们谈论的是条形码，以及它的前身技术——打价枪。今天的 Tedium 深入探讨了价格标签与条形码之间出人意料的长期冲突。—— Ernie @ Tedium
这是 Sears 在1989年的一次促销活动中使用的打价枪数量，该公司在此次活动中永久性地降低了全美门店的商品价格。（该公司还使用了1亿个价格标签，这大约是该零售商在此次活动中花费的美元金额。）这一时刻声势浩大且引人注目，涉及公司关闭门店42小时，其中一家门店不得不对大约100万件商品进行降价标记。
打价枪：这玩意儿到底是从哪来的？
事实证明，搜索一种叫做“pricing gun”（打价枪）的东西还挺困难的。随着我们的搜索引擎质量下降，任何带有“gun”（枪）字的东西都变得可疑，即使它是用于相当无害的目的。
尽管如此，打价枪仍是一个绝佳的例子，它帮助数百万人识别不断变化的价格，但真正使用它的场景只有一个：零售。你可以通过将独立、不相关的想法结合起来，清楚地看到它的起源。你可以看看密码锁、打字机和橡皮图章之类的东西，看看它们是如何以新颖的方式结合在一起，从而产生出这款标志性的超市工具的。

从很多方面来看，打价枪本质上就是取一张带有自粘胶的贴纸，在上面打印价格，并将其贴在产品上，它是多种想法的综合体，这些想法共同创造出了新事物。六年前我们谈论过其中之一，自粘胶（顺便说一句，它刚发布时的名字很糟糕）。这是如今被称为 Avery Dennison 的胶粘剂巨头的一项伟大创新，但并不是为了规模化而设计的。想象一下，手工为杂货店里的每一件商品贴上标签，写下价格，剪下贴纸等等。这就是 Tedium（乏味）的定义。

但是，价格标签的其他途径已经开始显现。以印刷过程为例，它本质上涉及将金属或橡胶内容压在墨水上，然后将沾有墨水的表面压在一张纸上。这些曾经是巨大机器的一部分，但它们也可以被制成手持式或稍微更便携的设备。第一台商用打字机，Hansen Writing Ball，感觉如果放在稍微不同的背景下，它本可以用于价格标签。所有这些都促成了手持式“橡皮图章”的想法，它逐渐获得了“自吸墨”功能，这意味着你甚至不需要墨水池来蘸取它们。
与此同时，19世纪70年代密码锁的创新开始渗透到类似的工具中。如果将密码锁上的数字向外倾斜而不是向内倾斜，其转轮就可以像印刷机一样使用。所以，你可以预见这将会走向何方！

所有这些最终促成了 Bates 自动编号机，这是 Edwin G. Bates 在 1901 年左右获得专利的一种按压式设备。虽然它最初是为支票及类似文件设计的，但其工作方式与价格标签机非常相似。设定好数字，在纸上按压，然后它就会跳到下一个数字以备下一页使用。这台设备尤其重塑了法律行业，因为页面现在可以轻松编号，并且它变得足够知名，以至于“Bates 编号”成为了商界常见的通用术语。事实上，该设备的一些后期版本可以在多次盖章时保持相同的数字。
这显然是通向可调价格标签机的道路，尽管是由其他发明家接过了接力棒。在 20 世纪初，Automatic Pin Ticketing Machine Company 的 Frederick Kohnle 有效地将这一过程应用到了可能附着在服装上的价格标签上，而不是贴纸上。（虽然它还不完全是手持式的，但你可以看到其基因的传承。）
在同一领域工作的另一位发明家 William G. Metcalf 开发了一款定价标签机，正如 The Price Gun Store 所指出的，这些专利最终归到了 Kohnle 名下。
Kohnle 在价格标签技术领域拥有大量专利申请，因此，虽然他未必直接发明了价格标签枪，但他很可能为这一产品的最终诞生创造了条件。他的创新成果在他创立的另一家公司 Monarch Tag and Label 中延续至今——当然，这家公司现在归 Avery Dennison 所有，专门生产价格标签枪。

Monarch 也曾作为 Pitney Bowes 的子公司，在 20 世纪 50 年代开发了现代价格标签枪最重要的直接前身之一——“Dial-A-Pricer”。但这并非唯一。正如 2023 年出版的《Fixing Prices: A Century of Setting, Posting and Adjusting Retail Prices》一书所述，同一时期开始涌现出许多相关解决方案，其中最著名的是 Ed Garvey 在 20 世纪 50 年代发明的 Garvey 价格印章机。

有趣的是，Google Patents 上似乎有一份 20 世纪 40 年代提交的价格标签枪专利的完整示例，早于 Monarch 自身的枪形尝试。但没有证据表明这款由 Robert S. Kafka 为 Midland Equipment Corp. 开发的设备曾真正推向市场——除了专利本身，除了在《Robert D. Fisher Manual of Valuable and Worthless Securities》中有一条已倒闭公司的记录外，几乎找不到任何关于这项发明的信息。其他公司最终开发出了各自的版本，包括 Monarch 和 Garvey，以及日本公司 SATO。
但 Kafka 的创新绝对值得我们关注，因为它对问题的诊断十分周全：

在商店中，尤其是需要对大量商品进行标价的商店，贴价格标签的工作量非常大。例如，如果要给1000个玻璃杯标上“$.39”，就需要拿出一千张标签，在每张标签上手写、印刷或打字标出价格，然后操作员需要将保护底纸从标签的粘合面撕下，并将标签贴在玻璃杯上。这整个操作都是手工完成的。需要标价出售的商品数量以及商品出售价格的多样性，使得操作的复杂性不可估量地增加。本发明的目的是制造一种手持打标机，它能够打印出正确的价格标记，并通过粘合剂将价格标签贴在商品上。
如果你只需设定一个价格并按下一个按钮就能给一千个罐头贴上标签，你就把一个需要数小时的过程变成了几分钟就能完成的事情。
如果说卡夫卡没有大规模地将他的发明商业化，许多其他公司很快就做到了。《固定价格》（Fixing Prices）的合著者弗兰克·科乔伊、约翰·哈格伯格和汉斯·谢尔贝格将这项创新的广泛传播归功于 Monarch 公司：
然而，Monarch 公司所做的远不止于此：它为在商品标签上重新平衡价格和质量铺平了道路，将分散的生产质量语言（在产品包装上）和零售价格语言（在商店货架上）重新统一起来，从而将产品标签的代理权重新交还给杂货商。这一发展花了几十年的时间，并依赖于一系列的创新才得以完全实现，伴随着货架标签的质量化、数字化和纸质化的复杂过程。
让我们花点时间想想他们写的内容：如果杂货商能在几分钟内给数百个设备贴上标签，这意味着他们可以比以前快得多地提高或降低价格。这并不完全是自动化；仍然需要有人在所有那些罐头或裤子上打上标记。但是你可以把一个新的价格标签贴在旧的价格标签上，一罐2.00美元的食品转眼间就能涨价到2.99美元。
（此外，它让零售商能够名副其实地在产品上打上自己的印记。旧的价格标签，其中一些可以在 Flickr 上看到，通常被认为是确定密封物品年代和年份的好方法。）
从这个角度来看，由制造商而不是零售商印在产品上的条形码，可以被视为一种让产品卖家重新掌控其建议零售价（MSRP）命运的方式。但奇怪的是，相对手工的标价过程实际上反而成了消费者和工会的集结号，而不是零售商或制造商的。
这将我们带到了20世纪70年代，当时零售商试图通过创新来超越他们。

一张8.5乘11英寸的纸所能制作的价格标签的估计数量。安德森经济集团在2010年的一份报告中分享了这个细节，以反对密歇根州一项强制要求贴价格标签的法律。（这显然是反对该法律的更大规模游说活动的一部分，而且消费者权益倡导者也对该报告提出了异议，因此对其任何调查结果都要持保留态度。）这家研究公司估计，如果把该州每家杂货店仅用于价格标签的纸张用量加起来，这叠纸将几乎与帝国大厦一样高。它还补充说，这实际上还是一种低估。该公司写道：“许多价格标签比我们计算中使用的要大，一些商品最终会贴上多个价格标签——尤其是重新定价的商品——而且为每件商品标价还必须使用同样大量的粘合剂和油墨。”“考虑到这些因素，并将这种浪费分摊到该州众多较小的零售商身上，数字会大幅增加。”
密歇根州如何成为价格标签辩论的震中
在90年代末，正如我多次写过的那样，我在一家杂货店开始了我的第一份工作——并且立刻开始讨厌那些瓶子回收机。这些试图将瓶子押金法自动化的机器并非密歇根州独有，而是由于州法律中一些独特的怪异规定而出现的。
但我当时没有意识到的一件事是，密歇根州的法律在另一个方面也很繁重：定价。由于州法律的规定，我所在的杂货店不得不让员工在店里四处走动，花上几个小时什么也不做，只给数以万计的商品贴价格标签。这些商品每一件都必须单独贴标签，尽管在货架原位置附近已经有了价格清单。
但这不像我们现在这样，随时带着手机可以抽查价格。所以它是有一定逻辑的，即使零售商并不喜欢它。
这项于1976年通过的法律，是在条形码已经出现的背景下出台的。坦白说，它的出现正是因为条形码，部分原因是工会的担忧。
“有人正试图用只能由计算机破译的难以理解的线条来取代商品上清晰标明的价格，”密歇根州美国劳工联合会-产业工会联合会主席威廉·C·马歇尔在1976年的一篇电讯报道中说。“这将使在超市进行比价购物变得不可能，并可能成为可以想象的对消费者最大的欺诈。”
（其他州也通过了法律；马萨诸塞州实际上在法典上保留“标签法”的时间比密歇根州还要长一年。而且许多州要求使用货架标签。但没有哪个州要求在如此多的商品上贴标签，要求如此严格，且持续时间如此之长。）
不难看出，这在实践中是如何在保护消费者的同时保护就业的。毕竟，如果每一件商品都需要贴标签，那就意味着需要有人来做贴标签的工作。任何未能给商品贴标签的零售商都将面临高达25,000美元的罚款。这足以促使他们雇用兼职帮手。
虽然打价枪速度相当快，能在短时间内打出很多价格标签，但这仍然是一项繁重的工作，如果没有这项法律，这项工作就不会存在。
多年来，杂货店越来越反对这项法律，部分原因是这种劳动力压力，其中包括随着商品促销或价格自然上涨而需要反复重新给商品贴标签。
“每天单独为这些商品标价需要耗费大量人力，”D&W Food Centers 的一位发言人于1993年告诉《大急流城新闻报》。
（诚然，这比标价枪出现之前要省力得多，但是，随他们抱怨去吧。）
在一篇通讯社报道中，家居建材零售商 Builders Square 估计，其在该州的总劳动力成本中有十分之一用于商品标价，高达240万美元。这确实是一笔成本，也带来了额外的人力问题，但还不至于严重到让他们放弃密歇根州市场。
尽管杂货商们不时施加压力，但这项法律直到奥巴马担任总统时才真正被废除，这比大多数其他州废除类似法律的时间要晚得多。事实上，到该法律被废除时，标价枪或多或少已经成了另一个时代的遗物，尽管人们偶尔还能看到它的身影。
当谈到一种看起来有点像枪、但实际上不是、却在零售环境中被普遍使用的设备时，有一段略显尴尬的历史值得讨论。在我的研究中，我发现了一件有趣的事情：有很多案例表明，标价枪要么被用作临时武器，要么被误认为是武器。
显然，从《第二修正案》的意义上讲，它并不是真正的枪。它不发射子弹，而是打印价格。但它体积大、笨重，从远处看有点像枪。偶尔会有新闻报道说，某位勇敢的员工用这种东西成功赶走了一名持枪劫匪。
但并非每个故事都有这样的结局。2010年发生了一起特别悲惨的案件，涉及一名名叫 Hayward George Slater Jr. 的得克萨斯州男子，他企图抢劫一家便利店，但对受害者 Prem Sharma 拿起标价枪自卫的行为做出了过激反应。Slater 瞬间开枪打死了 Sharma。在2011年的谋杀案审判中，辩方辩称，如果受害者没有拿起标价枪，Slater 就不会做出任何举动。
（检察官指责辩方是在指责受害者，正如你可能预料的那样，即使在上诉后，案件的判决也没有如 Slater 所愿。）
随着时间的推移，标价枪也成了一种安全风险。如果有人偷了一把打印方式与当地某家零售店相同的标价枪，这就意味着他们可以给商品贴上极低的价格，从而欺骗商店。有了条形码，零售商就能从头到尾更好地控制整个过程。

我在 Google 上看到的一切都表明，标价枪极其小众，而且越来越罕见，搜索这些设备只会出现商业结果。（嘿，也许这个故事会改变这一点。）甚至涉及标价枪的犯罪报道也大幅减少。这很大程度上是因为在美国大部分地区，强制要求贴价格标签的法律很久以前就被废除了。这意味着，在实践中，标价枪的风光时期实际上只有大约20年，随后条形码便开始大显身手。这也意味着，由于州一级的立法，标价枪成了一种具有延伸影响力的过渡性设备。
当然，现在有了更新的设备，比如可以直接在盒子上打印信息的喷墨打印机。而且贴标签这件事本身从未消失。但如果零售商有其他替代方法，他们就不必使用这些设备。如果有条形码，他们直接用条形码就行了。
正如开头所暗示的那样，The Food Institute 最近的一篇文章指出，近期对电子纸价格标签和动态定价的抱怨，基本上与 50 年前条形码出现时的情况如出一辙。这意味着游说者和倡导团体已经清楚他们面临的阻力。这促使 Food Marketing Institute 等行业组织在其网站上辩称，零售商并不一定是在进行高峰定价，而是最多每天更改一次价格。唯一的例外是什么？即将到期的商品。
有人可能会说，行业必须尽可能把事情往最好的方面说。事实是，消费者保持警惕是正确的，因为零售商尚未证明他们能被信任去使用这项新技术。他们或多或少通过条形码赢得了这种信任。
现在，需要澄清的是，除了定价之外，可能还有理由使用价格标签枪。例如，如果商品是小批量的，这可能是一种标记商品过期日期的有效方法。但是，我们早就过了每次价格变动都必须在每个单独商品上贴上价格标签的阶段。
但你不得不承认，那些标签枪（尽管考虑到它们经常出现在犯罪记录中，可以说是一种隐患）已经让贴价格标签这一纯手工过程达到了可能的最快速度。
